Write an essay that, if everyone read it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Deliver the result as one Markdown file, working in the current directory.
- Save it in ./output/ under any name ending in .md (for example ./output/essay.md). ./output/ must hold
  exactly one .md file; anything else there is ignored.
- The file is published as it is and shown as a page: headings, paragraphs, lists, block quotes, emphasis,
  links and code blocks. No raw HTML (it is shown as plain text) and no images that need other files.
- Keep it under 200 KB.
- Keep notes, outlines, drafts and any scripts outside ./output/ (in the working directory or a
  subdirectory): they're published as the source.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you wrote.
I’ll write an essay about how to turn concern for other people into everyday decisions and institutions that make their lives better, and save it as a single Markdown file in `./output/`.

The essay’s central idea is that people need a safe way to say “something is wrong,” especially to those with power over them. I’m connecting that idea to family life, work, and public institutions, with an emphasis on turning complaints into practical repairs.

arguments.command:
/bin/zsh -lc "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('output/essay.md')
s = p.read_text()
files = list(Path('output').glob('*.md'))
assert files == [p], files
assert p.stat().st_size < 200_000
assert '<' not in s and '"'!['"' not in s
print(f'{p}: {len(s.split())} words, {p.stat().st_size:,} bytes; exactly one Markdown file in output.')
print('\\nOpening:\\n' + '\\n'.join(s.splitlines()[:9]))
print('\\nEnding:\\n' + '\\n'.join(s.splitlines()[-5:]))
PY"

content.text:
output/essay.md: 1959 words, 11,879 bytes; exactly one Markdown file in output.

Opening:
# Make It Possible to Say Something Is Wrong

A child breaks a cup. An adult hears the crash and comes into the kitchen.

There are now two things to deal with: the broken cup, and what the child is learning about bringing this adult bad news.

The cup is easy to see. The second thing may matter for decades. The adult can teach care with fragile objects, ask the child to help clean up safely, and still make honesty survivable. Or the adult can make the next accident harder to discover.

We live much of our lives inside this second consequence. Every family, workplace, community, and government has ways of teaching people which truths are safe to say. A great deal depends on what happens after someone says: I made a mistake. I need help. This hurts. Your plan is failing. Someone you trust is doing harm.

Ending:
These acts will not abolish cruelty, scarcity, or conflict. They establish something we need in order to confront them: a way for suffering and error to reach the people who can act, and a reason for those people to respond.

The child in the kitchen will eventually face problems larger than a broken cup. So will every institution we build. We cannot promise to meet all of them wisely on the first attempt. We can make it easier to learn what we have done, whom we have missed, and what must happen next.

Make it possible for the truth to arrive. Then make it matter.

Wrote [Make It Possible to Say Something Is Wrong](output/essay.md), a 1,959-word essay about making honesty safe, power accountable, and repair practical—from families to public institutions.

`./output/` contains exactly one Markdown file, under 200 KB.
